question.prompt: All the high schools in a large school district are involved in a fundraiser selling T-shirts. Which of the choices below is logically equivalent to the statement “No school bigger than Euclid HS sold more T-shirts than Euclid HS”?

choices.content:
All schools smaller than Euclid HS sold fewer T-shirts than
Euclid HS.

No school that sold more T-shirts than Euclid
HS is bigger than Euclid HS.

All schools bigger than Euclid HS sold fewer T-shirts than
Euclid HS.

All schools that sold fewer T-shirts than Euclid HS are smaller
than Euclid HS.

All schools smaller than Euclid HS sold more T-shirts than
Euclid HS.

solutions.title: Use the contrapositive
solutions.explanation:
The original statement allows a bigger school to tie Euclid HS in sales. It only forbids a school from being both bigger and selling more.

Suppose a school sold more T-shirts than Euclid HS. That school cannot be bigger than Euclid HS, because having both properties would violate the original statement. Therefore,

“No school that sold more T-shirts than Euclid HS is bigger than Euclid HS.”

This is choice B. It is the contrapositive of the original statement: “bigger implies not selling more” becomes “selling more implies not bigger.”

The implication also works backward. If choice B holds, then a bigger school cannot have sold more T-shirts, since such a school would contradict B. Thus the statements are equivalent.

The answer is \(\boxed{\text{B}}\).

solutions.title: Test the other choices
solutions.explanation:
One counterexample is enough to show that a proposed equivalent statement fails. Equality in T-shirt sales gives particularly useful examples here.

Imagine Euclid HS has \(100\) students and sells \(20\) shirts. Suppose every other school sells at most \(20\) shirts. The original statement is then true, regardless of the schools' sizes. This district may include:

- A school with \(90\) students that sells \(20\) shirts. It is smaller but sells neither fewer nor more shirts, so choices A and E are false.
- A school with \(110\) students that sells \(20\) shirts. It is bigger but does not sell fewer shirts, so choice C is false.
- A school with \(120\) students that sells \(19\) shirts. It sells fewer shirts but is bigger, so choice D is false.

Thus A, C, D, and E can all fail while the original statement holds.

Choice B forbids exactly the same situation as the original: a school that is both bigger than Euclid HS and sells more shirts. Consequently, the equivalent statement is \(\boxed{\text{B}}\).
